traveler: Paul the Apostle (Saul of Tarsus, Sha'ul, Paulos)
title: The Basket at the Wall: Saul of Tarsus, the Road, and the Roads After It
years: c. 5 CE - c. 65 CE (both ends reconstructed; no ancient source dates either)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tarsus, birth in the Cilician capital
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. No ancient source states his birth year; the range c. 5 BCE to 5 CE is a modern back-calculation, and month and day are defaulted. Acts 21:39 and 22:3 name Tarsus and the Roman citizenship; Paul's own letters never name his birthplace.
stops.campa: Tarsus stands where the Cydnus comes down from the Cilician Gates to the sea, capital of a Roman province, a city of linen-weavers and lecture halls. A son is born there to a Jewish household of the tribe of Benjamin and given the name Saul, after the first king Israel ever had. He is circumcised on the eighth day. Greek is what he hears in the street and the Law is what he hears at home. His own letters will name the tribe, the circumcision and the party he joined, and never once name the city he was born in.
stops.quote: circumcised on the eighth day, a member of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.
suggested_refs: The well and the former church of St Paul in old Tarsus, shown as the site of the family house and now a museum; no ancient documentation ties the plot to him
Strabo, Geography 14.5.13, on Tarsus and its schools

stops.name: Jerusalem, at the feet of Gamaliel
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and disputed. The Jerusalem schooling under Gamaliel appears only in Acts 22:3, whose punctuation is itself ambiguous, and Paul's own letters never name Gamaliel or a Jerusalem upbringing. No site for such a school is located; the coordinate is a generic Jerusalem pin. Year, month and day are ordering devices only.
stops.campa: The speech Acts puts in his mouth years later, shouted in Aramaic from the barracks steps, claims a Jerusalem education: brought up in this city, at the feet of Gamaliel, taught strictly in the ancestral law. Gamaliel is the great Pharisaic teacher of the generation. In everything Paul himself writes, across thousands of words about his own past, that name never appears, and neither does Jerusalem as a boyhood city. What he does claim in his own hand is the party and the fervour: as to the law a Pharisee, advancing beyond his contemporaries, extreme for the traditions of his fathers.
stops.quote: I am a Jew born in Tarsus in Cilicia but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated strictly according to our ancestral law, being zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
suggested_refs: Acts 5:34-39, the same Gamaliel counselling the Sanhedrin to leave the new sect alone

stops.name: Jerusalem, the cloaks at Stephen's stoning
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Paul's own letters attest that he persecuted the assembly violently and name no victim, court or death. The Stephen scene is Acts 7:58-8:3 alone; Acts gives no location for the stoning, and the traditional site is contested between the Kidron near the Lions' Gate and the church on the Nablus Road north of the Damascus Gate, so the coordinate is a generic Jerusalem pin. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Witnesses at a stoning strip to throw, and someone has to hold the coats. Acts puts the young man Saul at the edge of the crowd doing exactly that while Stephen is killed outside the city, and then sends him from house to house dragging off men and women to prison. Paul's own hand confirms the substance and none of the scene. He writes that he was violently persecuting the church of God and trying to destroy it, and that he advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age. He names no victim, no court, no charge, and no death.
stops.quote: I was violently persecuting the church of God and was trying to destroy it. I advanced in Judaism beyond many among my people of the same age, for I was far more zealous for the traditions of my ancestors.
suggested_refs: The two rival sites of Stephen's stoning at Jerusalem, at the Lions' Gate and on the Nablus Road, neither fixed by any ancient text

segments.name: The Road, and the Years Nobody Wrote Down

stops.name: Road to Damascus, the light near Kaukab
stops.date_confidence: the call itself is attested in Paul's own words (Galatians 1:15-16, 1 Corinthians 15:8) with no road, no light and no voice; the roadside scene is Acts, narrated three times with variant details. The site southwest of the city near the village of Kaukab is late local tradition and appears nowhere in Acts. Conventional date range 31-36 CE; year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He is carrying letters and travelling north to arrest people. Acts tells the rest three separate times and cannot keep it identical: a light out of heaven at midday, a voice using his name twice, men standing speechless, three days without sight, a hand leading him into the city. Paul, writing to the Galatians about the same event, describes no road and no light. He says God was pleased to reveal his Son in him, so that he might proclaim him among the gentiles. Neither version cancels the other, and they do not describe the same afternoon.
stops.quote: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
suggested_refs: The three Damascus-road narratives of Acts 9, 22 and 26, compared for their variants
The chapel near Kaukab, southwest of Damascus, shown as the place of the vision

stops.name: Damascus, the house of Ananias
stops.date_confidence: the baptism and the disciple Ananias are Acts 9:10-19; Paul never mentions Ananias in any surviving letter. The crypt venerated as the house is post-biblical site tradition. Coordinate from Wikipedia, 'Chapel of Saint Ananias'. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A disciple named Ananias is told in a vision to go to the street called Straight, to the house of Judas, and lay hands on the man from Tarsus who has come to arrest him. He objects; he has heard what this man does to people. He goes anyway. Something falls from Saul's eyes, he eats, and within days he is in the Damascus synagogues arguing that Jesus is the Son of God, which startles everyone who knows why he came. A crypt below the modern street level, near the old wall, is shown as the house. Excavation there in 1921 turned up a Byzantine church of the fifth or sixth century.
suggested_refs: The street called Straight, the Roman decumanus of Damascus, still running east to west through the old city
The Chapel of Saint Ananias and the 1921 excavation beneath it

stops.name: Arabia, the Nabataean silence
stops.date_confidence: attested in Paul's own words (Galatians 1:17) that he went at once into Arabia and afterward returned to Damascus. Neither destination nor activity nor duration is stated. Arabia here probably means the Nabataean kingdom, and the coordinate, Petra, marks that kingdom rather than any known stop. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He does not go up to Jerusalem. He says so twice in the same sentence, as if the objection is already coming at him: he conferred with no human being, he went to none of those who were apostles before him, he went away at once into Arabia. What he did there he never says. How long he stayed is not stated. Arabia here is most likely the Nabataean kingdom, and the one later trace of him in it is hostile: the ethnarch of King Aretas sets a watch on Damascus to have him seized.
stops.quote: But when the one who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the gentiles, I did not confer with any human, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were already apostles before me, but I went away at once into Arabia, and afterward I returned to Damascus.
suggested_refs: The Nabataean kingdom under Aretas IV, reaching from the Hauran to the Hejaz

stops.name: Damascus, the basket at Bab Kisan
stops.date_confidence: attested in Paul's own words (2 Corinthians 11:32-33). Usually dated before the death of Aretas IV in 40 CE, which makes it one of the few external anchors in his early chronology; the exact year is not stated, and month and day are defaulted. Bab Kisan's identification of the window is site tradition, not archaeology.
stops.campa: The governor under King Aretas sets a watch on the gates of Damascus to take him. His people put him in a basket, feed it out through a window in the wall, and lower him down the outside in the dark. Paul tells this himself, in a letter, at the end of a list of beatings and shipwrecks he is offering as credentials against rivals who prefer visions and letters of recommendation. A gate on the southeast side, raised under Rome to Saturn and later called Bab Kisan, is where the city keeps the memory of it.
stops.quote: In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped from his hands.
suggested_refs: Bab Kisan and the Chapel of Saint Paul built into it, Damascus old city
The reign of Aretas IV of Nabataea, ended 40 CE, the outer limit for this escape

stops.name: Jerusalem, fifteen days with Cephas
stops.date_confidence: attested in Paul's own words (Galatians 1:18-19), dated by him only as three years after the call, with the starting point of that count disputed. Month and day are ordering devices; the coordinate is a generic Jerusalem pin.
stops.campa: Three years after the revelation he goes up at last, and the visit is small: fifteen days in the house of Cephas, and of the other apostles nobody except James, the Lord's brother. Paul counts those days out in writing years later because the number is an argument. He did not get his gospel from these men. He came to make their acquaintance, briefly, after he already had it. In this period the churches of Judea never see his face; they hear only that the man who used to hunt them is preaching the faith he was trying to destroy.
suggested_refs: Galatians 1-2, Paul's own chronology of his Jerusalem visits, set against the four visits of Acts

stops.name: Tarsus, the unrecorded decade in Syria and Cilicia
stops.date_confidence: attested in Paul's own words (Galatians 1:21-24) that he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia; Acts 11:25 adds that Barnabas later fetched him from Tarsus. The length of the gap, roughly a decade, is inferred from Paul's own fourteen-year count and is not stated anywhere. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Then the record closes for something like ten years. He says only that he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, which means home. No letter survives from this stretch, no city is named, no congregation is credited to it, and Acts skips it entirely. When the silence breaks it is because somebody else comes looking. Barnabas, needing a second teacher for a mixed assembly at Antioch, travels to Tarsus to find him. Acts does not say how he knew where to look.
suggested_refs: The gap between Galatians 1:21 and Acts 11:25, the longest undocumented stretch of his adult life

stops.name: Antioch on the Orontes, the year of teaching
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Antioch year and the coining of the name Christians rest on Acts 11:25-26 alone; Paul's own letters never describe the year, though they treat Antioch as a base. This dossier's geography lens tagged the same passage as attested, which is an inconsistency: a single witness makes it reconstruction. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Antioch is the third city of the empire, Greek-speaking and Syrian and Jewish at once, packed along the Orontes under Mount Silpius. Barnabas and Saul teach there together for a full year to an assembly that is not one thing ethnically and cannot be made one, and it is here, Acts says, that outsiders first find they need a word for these people and produce the word Christian. Every journey he makes from now on starts here, and here he comes back to report on it when it is done.
suggested_refs: Antioch on the Orontes, modern Antakya, and the street grid of the Seleucid foundation

stops.name: Jerusalem, the famine relief and the private hearing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a live contradiction left open here. Acts 11:27-30 has Barnabas and Saul carrying famine relief to Jerusalem under Claudius. Paul's own Galatians 2:1-10 has him going up after fourteen years with Barnabas and Titus to lay his gospel privately before James, Cephas and John. Whether these are one visit or two is unresolved in the scholarship and is not resolved here. Month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: A prophet named Agabus predicts a famine over the world, and the Antioch assembly takes up a collection for the brothers in Judea and sends it by the hands of Barnabas and Saul. That is the Acts account. Paul's own account of a Jerusalem trip in about these years says nothing about grain. It says he went up by revelation with Barnabas and Titus, laid his gospel privately before the men of repute, and that Titus, being Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised. One journey told twice, or two journeys? Nothing in either text decides it.
suggested_refs: The Claudian famine in Judea, and Josephus on Queen Helena of Adiabene's grain purchases during it

stops.name: Paphos, the proconsul and the magician
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Cyprus episode is Acts 13:4-12 alone, unsupported by anything in Paul's letters. The year is conventional for the first journey and month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: They land at Salamis on the east coast and work west across the island, preaching in the synagogues, and at Paphos they reach the governor's residence. The proconsul Sergius Paulus wants to hear them. A Jewish magician in his household, Bar-Jesus, called Elymas, argues against it. Saul looks at him and he goes blind, groping about for a hand to lead him, and the proconsul believes. From this scene forward Acts stops writing Saul and writes Paul, the Roman name. It gives no reason for the change, and it never uses the old name again.
suggested_refs: Nea Paphos, seat of the Roman proconsul of Cyprus, and its excavated governor's quarter

stops.name: Perga, John Mark turns back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 13:13 alone, which records the departure and gives no reason for it. The consequence, Paul's later refusal to take him again, is Acts 15:38. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: They cross from Cyprus to the Pamphylian coast and come up to Perga, and there John Mark leaves them and goes back to Jerusalem. Acts records the fact and not the cause. Homesickness, fear of the bandit country in the Taurus passes, a disagreement about how far the gentile mission should go, the text offers nothing at all. Two years later Paul will refuse to take the young man again and will lose Barnabas over the refusal, so whatever happened at Perga was not small to him. Mark's own view of it is recorded nowhere.
suggested_refs: The Hellenistic gate and colonnaded street of Perga in Pamphylia

stops.name: Pisidian Antioch, the synagogue sabbath
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 13:14-50 alone. The coordinate matches the pin already used for Antioch in Pisidia elsewhere in this corpus. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Up into the highlands, three and a half thousand feet, to a Roman colony of settled veterans with a synagogue in it. Invited to speak after the reading of the law and the prophets, Paul walks the congregation from Egypt to David to Jesus and lands on forgiveness of sins proclaimed through this man. The next sabbath, Acts says, nearly the whole city turns out. The synagogue that handed him the floor sees the crowd it did not invite. The leading men of the town drive him and Barnabas out of the district, and the two of them shake the dust off their feet at the gate.
suggested_refs: The foundations beneath the Byzantine church at Antioch in Pisidia, proposed as the synagogue of Acts 13

stops.name: Iconium, the house of Onesiphorus
stops.date_confidence: the preaching at Iconium and the flight from a plot to stone him are Acts 14:1-6. The house of Onesiphorus, the girl at the window and the physical description all come from the Acts of Paul and Thecla, a late second-century text; Tertullian, writing around 190, reports that its author, a presbyter in Asia, was convicted of composing it and removed from office. Legend, not testimony. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: At Iconium on the Lycaonian plain he speaks in the synagogue and the city splits in half, and when a plot forms to stone him he goes on to Lystra. A century later a second book grows over this visit like a shell. In it Paul lodges with Onesiphorus, and next door a girl named Thecla sits three days at her window without eating, listening to him preach chastity, and breaks off her engagement; her story runs from that window to the fire and the beasts. His own letters never mention her. The same book leaves the only physical description of him that anyone has.
stops.quote: a man little of stature, thin-haired upon the head, crooked in the legs, of good state of body, with eyebrows joining, and nose somewhat hooked, full of grace
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla 3, M. R. James trans.
suggested_refs: Acts of Paul and Thecla, late second century, the source of the standard iconographic type of Paul
Tertullian, On Baptism 17, on the deposition of the presbyter who wrote it
saint_thecla.journey.json, which follows the Iconium window from her side of the wall
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla 3, trans. M. R. James, earlychristianwritings.com (fetched 2026-08-24)
Tertullian, On Baptism 17, trans. S. Thelwall, newadvent.org (fetched 2026-08-24)

stops.name: Lystra, taken for Hermes, then stoned
stops.date_confidence: the Lystra episodes are Acts 14:8-20. Paul's own letters attest a stoning without naming any place (2 Corinthians 11:25). The onward leg to Derbe and the return through these towns is Acts 14:20-21; the identification of Derbe with Kerti Huyuk, fixed by Michael Ballance in 1956 on a 157 CE inscription, is itself subject to controversy. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: A man lame from birth stands up, and the crowd shouts in Lycaonian that the gods have come down in the likeness of men. They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because Paul is the one doing the talking, and the priest of Zeus brings oxen and garlands to the gates. The two of them tear their clothes and run in among the people shouting that they are men of the same nature. Days later, with agitators arrived from Antioch and Iconium, the same city stones him and drags him outside the walls for dead. He gets up and walks on to Derbe.
stops.quote: Five times I have received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I received a stoning. Three times I was shipwrecked; for a night and a day I was adrift at sea.
suggested_refs: The mound of Lystra near Hatunsaray, identified by an inscribed Roman altar
Kerti Huyuk, proposed as Derbe on a 157 CE inscription, an identification still contested

stops.name: Jerusalem, the council on circumcision
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the council is Acts 15, conventionally dated c. 48-50 CE. Its relation to Paul's own account in Galatians 2:1-10 is disputed and is not settled here. Month and day are ordering devices; the coordinate is a generic Jerusalem pin.
stops.campa: The question is whether a gentile has to become a Jew first. Men from Judea have been telling the Antioch converts that without circumcision, according to the custom of Moses, they cannot be saved, and the matter goes up to Jerusalem, to James and Cephas and John. Paul and Barnabas report what has been happening among the nations. The ruling comes back down: no circumcision, no whole yoke of the law, only abstention from what has been offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. The letter carrying those terms goes back down to Antioch in the hands of Judas Barsabbas and Silas.
suggested_refs: The apostolic decree of Acts 15:23-29 and its variant readings in the Western text

stops.name: Antioch, Cephas rebuked to his face
stops.date_confidence: attested in Paul's own words (Galatians 2:11-14), which preserve the rebuke and never state its outcome. The subsequent quarrel with Barnabas over John Mark is Acts 15:36-41. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Cephas comes to Antioch and eats with the gentile believers until men arrive from James, and then he stops, and draws back, and the other Jews there follow him, and even Barnabas is carried along with the pretence. Paul says he opposed him to his face in front of everyone, because he stood condemned. The letter that reports this never says who won. What the record does show is that Paul and Barnabas part soon after over whether to take John Mark again. Barnabas sails to Cyprus with his cousin and Paul takes Silas overland.
suggested_refs: Galatians 2:11-14, the only first-hand record of a quarrel between two apostles

stops.name: Lystra, Timothy joins
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 16:1-3 alone. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Back over the Taurus into the towns of the first circuit, and at Lystra, the city that stoned him, he picks up a companion. Timothy has a Jewish mother who believes and a Greek father, and the brothers at Lystra and Iconium speak well of him. Paul takes him, and then circumcises him, on account of the Jews in those places, all of whom knew that his father was Greek. The man who had just refused at Jerusalem to let Titus be circumcised performs the operation here himself. Acts records it in a single verse and passes on without comment.
suggested_refs: Acts 16:3 against Galatians 2:3, the two circumcision decisions set side by side

segments.name: Macedonia, Achaia, and the First Letter

stops.name: Philippi, Lydia and the inner cell
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 16:9-34, including the night vision at Troas that sends the party across to Macedonia. No prison structure at Philippi has been identified with the narrative. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: A man of Macedonia stands in a night vision at Troas and asks him to come over and help, and he crosses. At Philippi, a Roman colony, the first person who listens is Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira; her household is baptized and her house becomes the lodging. Then he drives a divining spirit out of an enslaved girl and destroys her owners' income, and for that he and Silas are stripped, beaten with rods, and shut in the inner cell with their feet in the stocks. At midnight they are singing. An earthquake opens the doors.
suggested_refs: The forum and via Egnatia at Philippi, and the traditional baptistery of Lydia on the Zygaktes

stops.name: Thessalonica, three sabbaths and Jason's bail
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 17:1-9. That 1 Thessalonians went to this congregation soon after is standard scholarship, and its opening co-sender list (Paul, Silvanus, Timothy) is attested; that it is the earliest surviving Christian text and that it was written from Corinth are reconstructions, and its priority over Galatians is actively disputed. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Three sabbaths in the synagogue on the Egnatian Way, arguing from the scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead. Some believe, including a number of the leading women, and the rest raise a mob and go looking for him at the house of Jason. Not finding him, they drag Jason before the politarchs on a charge with teeth in it: these men act against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus. Jason posts security and Paul is sent away by night. The letter he writes back to these people is generally reckoned the oldest Christian writing that survives.
suggested_refs: The Thessalonian politarch inscription, confirming the rare civic title used in Acts 17:6
1 Thessalonians 1:1, whose co-senders are Paul, Silvanus and Timothy

stops.name: Berea, the scriptures examined daily
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 17:10-14 alone. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Sent on by night to Berea, off the main road, and the reception is different. Acts calls these Jews more noble than the ones at Thessalonica, because they take the message and then go and check it, searching the scriptures every day to see whether the things are so. Many believe, Greek women of standing among them and men as well. Then word gets back to Thessalonica and the agitators come the fifty miles to stir up the crowds here too. The brothers put Paul on the road toward the sea, and Silas and Timothy stay behind.
suggested_refs: The bema of Berea at modern Veria, a modern monument on the traditional preaching site

stops.name: Athens, the Areopagus and the unknown god
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 17:16-34. Scholars dispute whether he addressed the actual council of the Areopagus or spoke informally on the hill, and the speech as it stands is generally credited to the author of Acts. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Waiting alone in a city full of statues, he argues daily in the market with whoever is there, Epicureans and Stoics included, and they take him up to the Areopagus to explain the foreign divinities. He starts from an altar he says he found inscribed to an unknown god and works toward a God who made the world and does not live in shrines built by hands, who is not far from any one of us. At the resurrection of the dead, some of them laugh. A few join him, among them a member of the council named Dionysius, and a woman named Damaris.
suggested_refs: The rock of the Areopagus below the Acropolis, and the bronze plaque of the speech set into its foot

stops.name: Corinth, the tentmakers' workshop
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 18:1-11 for the eighteen months and the partnership with Aquila and Priscilla. The stay is anchored indirectly by the Gallio proconsulship, which makes Corinth the firmest fixed point in his chronology. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He arrives with nothing and finds work. Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish artisans lately expelled from Rome under Claudius, are in the same leather trade, and he lodges with them and cuts and stitches beside them through the week and argues in the synagogue on the sabbath. The congregation he raises here is quarrelsome and litigious, split into factions over which teacher each of them belongs to. Eighteen months in one city, the longest he has stayed anywhere since Antioch.
stops.quote: Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unfit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am.
suggested_refs: The Claudian expulsion of Jews from Rome, dated by Suetonius to a disturbance over one Chrestus

stops.name: Corinth, before Gallio's tribunal
stops.date_confidence: the hearing is Acts 18:12-17. The proconsulship of Lucius Junius Gallio is independently fixed to c. 51-52 CE by the Delphi inscription, nine fragments of a letter of Claudius dated 52 CE referring to a recent report from Gallio. Through this hearing it anchors the Corinthian stay and, through that, the whole Pauline chronology. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: They bring him to the tribunal in the forum and accuse him of persuading people to worship God contrary to the law. Before Paul can open his mouth the proconsul cuts it off. If it were a crime or a piece of villainy, Gallio says, he would bear with them; but since these are questions about words and names and their own law, they can see to it themselves, and he drives them from the bema. The crowd then beats Sosthenes, the synagogue official, in front of the tribunal, and Gallio pays no attention to that either. Nine broken pieces of a letter of Claudius found at Delphi put him in Achaia across 51 and 52.
suggested_refs: The Delphi inscription, nine fragments of a letter of Claudius naming Gallio proconsul of Achaia
The bema in the Corinthian forum, excavated and identified with the tribunal of Acts 18
sources: Wikipedia summary of the Delphi/Gallio inscription (fetched 2026-08-24)

stops.name: Cenchreae, the head shaved for a vow
stops.date_confidence: attested in Acts 18:18, which gives the haircut and the vow and does not say what kind of vow it was; the identification as a Nazirite vow is inference. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: At the eastern harbour of Corinth, before sailing for Syria, he has his head shaved because of a vow. Acts drops the detail in passing and explains none of it: not which vow, not what he had asked for, not what he had been given. The obvious reading is a Nazirite vow, which would mean the apostle who was telling gentiles they need not keep the law was at that moment keeping a piece of it himself, in public, on a wharf, with Priscilla and Aquila standing there.
suggested_refs: The submerged harbour moles of Kechries, the eastern port of Corinth
Numbers 6:1-21, the law of the Nazirite and the shaving of the head

stops.name: Ephesus, the hall of Tyrannus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 19:1-20 for the two years in the lecture hall, the exorcisms and the burning of the magic books. That 1 Corinthians was written from Ephesus is attested by the letter itself (1 Corinthians 16:8), which also refers back to an earlier letter that does not survive. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Three months in the synagogue, then he takes the argument to a lecture hall belonging to one Tyrannus and holds the floor there daily for two years, until, Acts says, everyone living in Asia has heard the word. Handkerchiefs that have touched him are carried out to the sick. Converts pile their books of spells in the street and burn them, and somebody counts the value of the ashes at fifty thousand pieces of silver. From this city he writes to Corinth, answering their questions and their gossip, and mentions in passing an earlier letter to them that does not survive.
suggested_refs: The lost Corinthian correspondence: at least two letters of Paul's referred to in 1 and 2 Corinthians and never found

stops.name: Ephesus, the theatre and the affliction in Asia
stops.date_confidence: the riot is Acts 19:23-41; the affliction so heavy that he despaired of life is his own (2 Corinthians 1:8-10), which never says what it was. The phrase about fighting wild beasts at Ephesus (1 Corinthians 15:32) is generally read as metaphor, and no arena sentence is documented. The coordinate is the Ephesus site pin from Wikipedia; an earlier draft of this dossier placed it on the Library of Celsus, two hundred metres from the Great Theatre. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis, calls the trade together and points out that this preaching is emptying their workshops. The city fills up; they seize two of Paul's companions and pour into the great theatre, and for about two hours the crowd shouts that Artemis of the Ephesians is great, most of them not knowing why they came. The town clerk finally warns them that Rome will call this sedition. Paul writes about Asia afterward only that he was crushed utterly, beyond his strength, so that he despaired of life itself. He does not say what happened.
stops.quote: a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, to keep me from being too elated. Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me, but he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.'
suggested_refs: The Great Theatre of Ephesus, seating some twenty-four thousand
The temple of Artemis at Ephesus and the trade in its silver shrines

stops.name: Cenchreae, Romans given to Phoebe
stops.date_confidence: Romans is commonly dated c. 56-58 CE and placed at Corinth. The letter itself names Tertius as its scribe and commends Phoebe, deacon of the church at Cenchreae, which is the ground for treating her as its courier; that she carried it is inference, not statement. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He is at the end of the eastern work and writing to a church he has never seen, to prepare a base for a mission further west. A man named Tertius takes it down and slips in a line greeting them in his own name, the only time a secretary of Paul's signs his own work. Somewhere in the middle of it stands the sentence telling them to be subject to the governing authorities. Phoebe, deacon of the assembly at the harbour, is commended to them in the closing lines; that commendation is the whole reason anyone thinks she carried the roll to Rome herself.
stops.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those authorities that exist have been instituted by God.
suggested_refs: Romans 16:1-2 and 16:22, the commendation of Phoebe and the signature of Tertius
Martin Luther's Wittenberg lectures on Romans, 1515-1516, and on Galatians, 1531, the reception that turned this letter into the trigger of the Reformation
Marcion's Apostolikon, c. 144, the earliest known collected edition of Paul's letters, surviving only in hostile quotation

stops.name: Troas, the boy in the third-floor window
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 20:6-12 alone. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The meeting runs long because he is leaving in the morning. Many lamps are burning in the upper room and the air goes thick, and a young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window of the third storey, sinks deeper and deeper into sleep as the talking goes past midnight, and falls. They pick him up dead. Paul goes down, throws himself on the boy, takes him in his arms and says his life is in him. Then he goes back upstairs, breaks bread, eats, and talks until daybreak. The boy is led away alive, and Acts adds that they were not a little comforted.
suggested_refs: Alexandria Troas, the harbour city of the Macedonian vision and the Eutychus night

stops.name: Miletus, the elders weep on the shore
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 20:17-38, whose farewell speech is generally regarded as the composition of the author of Acts rather than a transcript. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He sails past Ephesus to save time and sends thirty miles up the road for the elders instead, and they come down to the harbour to meet him. He tells them he is going to Jerusalem bound in the spirit, not knowing what will happen to him there except that in every city imprisonment and afflictions are waiting. He tells them they will not see his face again. He tells them savage wolves will get in among the flock after he leaves, and that some of them will come from among themselves. Then they kneel down on the beach and weep and put him on the ship.
suggested_refs: The Great Harbour Monument at Miletus, near which the meeting is traditionally placed

stops.name: Tyre, kneeling on the beach
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 21:3-6 alone. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The ship unloads its cargo at Tyre and they find disciples in the city and stay seven days, and those disciples tell him through the Spirit not to set foot in Jerusalem. He goes anyway. When the week is out the whole congregation walks him down out of the town, wives and children with them, and they all kneel on the sand and pray together. Then he boards and they go back to their houses. Acts does not record that anyone argued with him, and does not record what he said to them.
suggested_refs: The Roman harbour of Tyre and its causeway to the mainland

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, Agabus and the belt
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 21:8-14 alone. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He lodges at Caesarea with Philip the evangelist, who has four unmarried daughters who prophesy. The prophet Agabus comes down from Judea, takes Paul's own belt off him, ties his own feet and hands with it, and says that this is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and hand him over to the gentiles. Everyone in the room begs him not to go up. He answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die at Jerusalem, and they stop arguing and say only that the Lord's will be done.
suggested_refs: Caesarea Maritima, Herod's harbour city and the seat of the Roman procurators of Judea

stops.name: Jerusalem, seized at the Temple
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 21:27-22:2. The coordinate is the Temple Mount pin already in use elsewhere in this corpus. The barracks of Acts are traditionally identified with the Antonia fortress, an identification the sources do not confirm, though Josephus (Jewish War 5:243) describes a stairway from the fortress down into the Temple court matching Acts 21:40. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Jews from Asia see him in the Temple and shout that this is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place, and has now brought Greeks past the barrier into the holy ground. The doors are shut behind him and the crowd sets about killing him in the outer court. The tribune of the cohort comes down the steps with soldiers and takes him out of their hands in chains. On the stairs, half carried by the guard, he asks leave to speak, and addresses the mob below in Aramaic. They go quiet to hear it.
suggested_refs: The Greek warning inscription from the Temple balustrade, forbidding gentiles the inner courts on pain of death
Josephus, Jewish War 5:243, on the stairway from the Antonia into the Temple precinct

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, two years in Herod's praetorium
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 23:23-26:32 and 24:27-25:12. The bribe motive attributed to Felix is the narrator's, not an external record, and the two-year figure is Acts' alone. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Moved out of Jerusalem by night under two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, on word of a plot by forty men who have sworn not to eat or drink until he is dead. Then two years in the governor's residence at Caesarea, waiting. Felix sends for him often and hopes for money. Festus succeeds Felix and inherits the case. Agrippa hears him out of curiosity and tells Festus afterward that the man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. The appeal is his right as a citizen, and it moves the case to Rome.
suggested_refs: The promontory palace at Caesarea, identified as the praetorium of the Roman governors
The Pilate stone from the Caesarea theatre, the one epigraphic trace of the procurators there

stops.name: Fair Havens, the advice not taken
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 27:8-11. The coordinate is Kaloi Limenes on the south coast of Crete per Wikipedia; an earlier draft of this dossier placed it some nine kilometres inland to the northwest. A Byzantine church of the apostle stands at the bay, restored in the 1960s. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The season is late, past the Fast, and the Alexandrian grain ship has already lost weeks beating along the coast against the wind. In the roadstead at Fair Havens on the south side of Crete, Paul, a prisoner with no standing whatever to be consulted, tells them the voyage will end with injury and heavy loss, of the cargo and the ship and their lives. The centurion listens to the helmsman and the owner instead, because the harbour is a poor place to lie up for winter. They wait for a light southerly and go, and they get as far as the cape.
suggested_refs: Kaloi Limenes on the south coast of Crete, and the Byzantine chapel of the apostle above the bay

stops.name: Malta, the ship broken on the shoal
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 27:27-28:10. St Paul's Bay and the offshore islands are the traditional site, Maltese ecclesiastical tradition built on the Acts narrative rather than on archaeology; the grotto at Rabat shown as his winter shelter is likewise post-biblical. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Fourteen nights driven across open water with neither sun nor stars showing, and then, near dawn, sailors hearing surf and heaving the lead. They run her aground on a shoal between two seas, the bow sticking fast and the stern breaking up under the waves, and all two hundred and seventy-six aboard reach the beach, swimming or on planks and pieces of the ship. It is raining and cold and the islanders build a fire. He is gathering brushwood for it when a viper comes out of the heat and fastens on his hand. He shakes it into the flames.
suggested_refs: St Paul's Bay and the offshore islands on the northeast coast of Malta
St Paul's Grotto beneath Rabat, near Mdina, shown as the winter shelter
The healing of the father of Publius, chief man of the island, Acts 28:7-10

stops.name: Puteoli, seven days among believers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 28:11-14, including the three days at Syracuse and the touch at Rhegium. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Three months on Malta, then out on another Alexandrian ship that has wintered there, the Twin Brothers carved on her bow. Three days at Syracuse, a stop at Rhegium in the strait, then a southerly gets up and carries them to Puteoli in a single day. Puteoli is where Rome's grain comes ashore, and there are already believers living in it. They ask him to stay a week and the centurion allows it. Nobody records who brought word of the movement to this port, or when, or how long the believers there had been meeting before a prisoner off a grain ship walked up to them.
suggested_refs: The mole of Puteoli, terminus of the Alexandrian grain fleet

stops.name: Appii Forum, met on the Appian Way
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 28:15 alone. The coordinate marks the Forum of Appius on the Appian Way at the edge of the Pontine marshes; the Three Taverns lay some ten Roman miles nearer the city. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Word has gone up the road ahead of the escort. Roman believers walk out to meet the prisoner, some as far as the Forum of Appius, forty-three miles down the Appian Way at the edge of the Pontine marshes, others only to the Three Taverns nearer in. Both are posting stations on a road crowded with barge traffic and mule drivers, and neither is anybody's destination. He has been writing to these people for years and has never seen one of their faces. Acts says that when he saw them he thanked God and took courage. It is the last thing the book records him feeling.
suggested_refs: The Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns, posting stations on the Appian Way south of Rome

stops.name: Rome, two years at his own expense
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Acts 28:16-31, which ends without stating any outcome to the case. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He is allowed to live by himself with the soldier who guards him. Three days after arriving he calls the leading Jews of the city together and gives them his side of it; they answer that they have had no letters about him from Judea, but would like to hear what he thinks, since this sect is spoken against everywhere. They come to his lodging in numbers and he argues from morning until evening. Then two full years at his own expense, receiving everyone who comes, preaching openly and unhindered. There the book stops. It never says what the court decided.
suggested_refs: The abrupt ending of Acts at 28:31, and the long argument over why the author stops there

stops.name: Rome, the letters from confinement
stops.date_confidence: Philippians and Philemon are Paul's own and were written from confinement; which confinement is genuinely disputed among Rome, Caesarea and Ephesus, and placing them at Rome here does not settle the question. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: From custody he writes to Philippi that his chains have become known throughout the whole praetorium, and that this has made the work go forward rather than stop. And he writes a short private letter to a slaveholder named Philemon about a runaway named Onesimus, whom he is sending back: receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother. He does not order the man freed. He says he is bold enough to command it and would rather appeal, and mentions in passing that Philemon owes him his own self.
stops.quote: Perhaps this is the reason he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for the long term, no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother.
suggested_refs: Philemon, the shortest letter in the corpus and the only surviving private one
Papyrus 46, c. 175-225, the oldest substantial manuscript of the Pauline letters, split between the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin and the University of Michigan

stops.name: Spain, the journey that may never have happened
stops.date_confidence: unattested. Romans 15:24 and 15:28 prove only the intention. The phrase in 1 Clement about the farthest bounds of the West is ambiguous and may mean Spain or simply Rome seen from the eastern Mediterranean; explicit claims of a completed Spanish mission appear only later, in the Muratorian fragment and afterward. No Spanish community, inscription or letter confirms it. The coordinate marks the peninsula rather than any stop, and the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He told the Romans that he had no more room for work in these regions, that his ambition was never to build on another man's foundation, and that once he had delivered the collection to Jerusalem he would come through their city on his way to Spain. Whether he ever went, no source says. A letter written from Rome a generation later says he reached the limit of the West, and it does not say where that is. No Spanish church claims a foundation from him that anyone can check. The intention is documented. The arrival is not.
stops.quote: After preaching both in the east and west, he gained the illustrious reputation due to his faith, having taught righteousness to the whole world, and come to the extreme limit of the west, and suffered martyrdom under the prefects.
suggested_refs: The Muratorian fragment, the first text to state outright that Paul went to Spain

stops.name: Rome, the Mamertine
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and self-contradicting. The Mamertine prison below the Capitol is shown as his last cell, while the same tradition holds that he awaited trial in a house in the Campus Martius later built over by the church of San Paolo alla Regola. Neither is documented in any first-century source. Year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Under the Capitoline, beside the Forum, there is a two-level cell cut into rock, with a hole in the floor of the upper chamber through which the Republic lowered its enemies to be strangled. Rome shows it as the place he was held before execution. Rome also shows a house in the Campus Martius, later covered by a church, as the place where he awaited trial. The two traditions sit a mile apart and are told by the same city with the same confidence. Neither of them appears in any writing from the century he died in.
suggested_refs: The Carcer Tullianum below San Giuseppe dei Falegnami
San Paolo alla Regola, built over the house of the rival tradition

stops.name: Tre Fontane, the Ostian road
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The earliest witness, 1 Clement c. 96 CE, says only that he bore his testimony before the rulers and departed from the world, naming neither Rome nor Nero nor a manner of death. Eusebius and Tertullian carry an early Roman martyrdom tradition under Nero; the beheading, the site at Aquae Salviae and the three springs are later hagiographic development. Conventional range 64-67 CE; year, month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The developed story is precise exactly where the early sources are silent: Nero, the third milestone on the road to Ostia, a Roman citizen's beheading instead of the cross, and the severed head striking the ground three times, each fall opening a spring. The oldest surviving mention of his death, written from Rome about thirty years after it, says that he bore his testimony before the rulers and so departed from the world, and stops there. It names no emperor, no city and no blade.
suggested_refs: Tre Fontane Abbey at Aquae Salviae, and the three springs of the legend
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25, on the Neronian martyrdoms of Peter and Paul

stops.name: Rome, the sarcophagus under the Ostian basilica
stops.date_confidence: the burial on the Ostian Way is tradition; a modest memorial stood on the site by the early fourth century, consecrated 324 by Sylvester I, enlarged from 386 under Theodosius I. The sarcophagus beneath the papal altar, 2.55 by 1.25 by 0.97 metres and 1.37 metres below it, was confirmed by excavation announced 6 December 2006. Radiocarbon dating of bone fragments to the first or second century was announced by Benedict XVI on 28-29 June 2009, at the vigil and feast of Saints Peter and Paul; press and encyclopedia give the two dates. The date on this stop is the traditional burial, and month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: They bury him beside the road, and the grave keeps its address. A small memorial stands over it, then a basilica consecrated in 324, then a far larger one begun under Theodosius, then fifteen centuries, then a fire in 1823 started by a workman mending the copper gutters that takes down nearly all of it. Under the altar of the rebuilt church is a marble box inscribed to Paul, apostle and martyr. In 2006 archaeologists reached it. Bone fragments from inside were dated to the first or second century, and the head of the Vatican's own laboratory said the result neither confirms nor invalidates the attribution.
suggested_refs: The sarcophagus beneath the papal altar of San Paolo fuori le Mura, inscribed PAULO APOSTOLO MART
The purple linen laminated with gold, the grains of incense and the blue textile fibres found with the bone fragments
Ulderico Santamaria of the Vatican Museums diagnostics laboratory, on the limits of the 2009 result
sources: Wikipedia, 'Papal Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls' (fetched 2026-08-24)
